exercise1.prompt: Derived Columns: Each row as a share of the total

hiddenCases.name: a single row is all of the total
the total comes from the column
hiddenCases.describe: the column divided by its own sum

exercise1.hint: Divide the column by its own sum and multiply by 100. The division broadcasts the single total across every row.

exercise2.prompt: Derived Columns: The best rate, not the biggest total

hiddenCases.name: the biggest total can also be the best rate
the rate, not the total, decides
the vectorised form does the work
hiddenCases.describe: column operations rather than a loop

exercise2.hint: Build the rate as a column, then use idxmax to get the row label of the highest and read the region off it. Ranking on sales alone is what the third hidden case catches.

questions.prompt: How do you build a rate column from two existing columns?
questions.explain: Ordinary column arithmetic, aligned by index and applied to the whole column at once.

questions.prompt: What does df["x"] / df["x"].sum() give you?
choices: Each row’s share of the total
questions.explain: The single total is broadcast across every row, which is where a share or a percentage comes from.

choices: A new table with the column added
questions.explain: Which is what lets it sit in the middle of a chain and leave the original alone.

questions.prompt: Why prefer a rate to a total when comparing regions?
choices: The biggest total is often just the biggest region
questions.explain: Per head the ranking can reverse, and that reversal is usually the finding.
